When he asked why he’d be proud, it hit the weirdness underneath what I said — that I’d framed this whole thing like a performance, like I wanted applause for being bold and sexual, but really I was also embarrassed, sad, and a little lost in it. I could hear how much I was trying to make the moment mean “look, I’m capable, I can do this,” instead of admitting that I’d been alone in my own head and then unexpectedly met something real in myself.

[Decision] So I answered honestly: not because I was showing off, but because I actually did touch something real. I connected with myself in a way that doesn’t happen often, and I wanted to name that before I lost it behind the drama of the whole scene. I wanted to stop hiding in the story and say what mattered: even if it was messy and sad and weird, I was there with myself.

If he wants to sound impressed by her “methods,” fine, but he doesn’t get to use that as a wedge to undermine twenty years of treatment or make me defend myself to someone who hasn’t earned the right. I’m going to cut him down because that’s the only way to stop this bullshit from taking over. [Perception] You’re pointing at something uncomfortable: that I may have turned my own guilt into a reason to help other people, and that this room is part of that. [Decision] So I kept it light and let the focus drift toward a flattering explanation. It felt safer to make it about a noble motive than about my own burden, because going deeper risks exposing how attached I still am to being the one who had to forgive himself. Brevity lets me avoid being pinned down to the part of me that is still not ready to let that burden go completely.

I’m going to keep it at arm’s length and just give the one factual thing they can’t argue with — I’m on medication — because talking more feels pointless if they’re just going to steer me toward obvious questions and soft reassurance. I need to protect myself from getting my hopes up or being pushed into some “talk it out” route when what I really need is to get through this and keep my job.

I crack the door open and I see him. He's sitting at his desk. He's got his back to me. I don't know if he heard me. I was about to say something, but I didn't. I just stood there and I stared at the back of his head. Something about him... I don't know what it was... It broke my heart. Then I heard these footsteps coming up behind me, I turn around and it's my father. And he says, you know why he quit, don't you? I shook my head. And he gives me that look, that look that sees right through you. He says, He knew in three moves, Alex, You were gonna lose. He didn't want to beat his father in front of the whole family. context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Do you think he was right?

therapist_turn: Do you think he was right?
client_response: Yeah, I know he was right. That's my son to a tee.
internal:
[Perception] When he asked if my father was right, it landed different. It wasn’t just a story about my son quitting a chess game. It was my son seeing me clearly enough to spare me. Not pity like I first felt, but mercy. And that means he wasn’t rejecting me—he was trying not to wound me in front of everybody. The shame I felt wasn’t that I lost; it was that my boy had already figured out I was vulnerable before I could admit it myself.

[Decision] I can’t keep holding this like it was an insult. If I stay with that meaning, I lose him. If I accept that he was protecting me, then I can stop fighting the feeling and see the love in it. So I said yes—my father was right—because I finally understood what happened, and because I needed to own the truth before I could come back to my son differently.

[Decision] So I laid out the whole scene instead of staying with the vague stuff, because I needed the room to understand why this friendship feels so loaded and why I can’t just talk about it like it’s ordinary. I wanted to show the exact moment I felt exposed, and then the exact moment Leah rescued it by making a joke and getting everyone on her side. context.speaker: therapist
context.text: Sure.

client_response: Have you ever thought about... suicide?
internal:
[Perception] I heard the question and felt it land right on the place I’ve been trying not to look at. It wasn’t really about Gina, not in my head — it hit the part of me that’s been circling around David, around April, around all the ways I’ve been trying to be the one who holds everything together and still ending up too late, or wrong, or unable to fix what I touched. It made the whole thing feel stripped down to something simple and ugly: I can’t protect everyone, I can’t undo what happened, and I don’t even know how to talk about the part of me that wonders if any of this matters. Hope feels expensive right now. If I let myself want relief, I have to admit how exhausted and hopeless I am.

[Decision] So I pulled back. I decided not to go there, not really. It feels safer to stay vague, to ask it sideways, to make it about “have you ever thought about it?” instead of saying what I’m actually afraid to say about myself. If I keep it at a distance, I don’t have to risk being seen as broken, or have to believe there’s anything useful to do with this feeling anyway. Giving up a little felt like relief — not because I want this, but because trying to hold hope right now just feels like setting myself up to fail again.

That hit the exact thing I was trying not to let in — that I’m sitting here, exposed, being looked at, and I don’t really know what to do with that. He brought it back to me, to this room, which is exactly what makes me bristle and also why Patricia said he was good.

I didn’t want to sound like I was bolting, but I also didn’t want to admit outright that I was feeling cornered. “Not a nightmare” gave me some room, and “vague anxiety dream” kept it from sounding too dramatic. Then I added that Patricia was right and he’s easy to talk to because I was asking, without exactly asking, for him to stay easy. I was basically saying: keep going, but don’t pin me down too hard. I need this to feel less like interrogation and more like conversation, or I’m going to shut down.

If she hesitates, then I’ll know to be careful and not hand over too much. I’m trying to figure out whether this is a place where I can be understood without being treated like I’m fragile. Saying “Do you really think those things you wrote?” is my way of checking if she’s being honest with me before I let myself believe any of it.

internal:

[Decision] I decided I had to push back hard enough to keep the conversation grounded. If I let that framing stand, then suddenly my preferences become pathology and his bad coffee becomes my issue. So I challenged him—kept it light, but sharp—because I wanted him to know he was overreaching and that I wasn’t going to nod along to a story that doesn’t fit me.
